paragraphs.text: 1 The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel. 2 Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers? 3 Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation. 4 That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpillar eaten.

The prophet opened the book with the words: “The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel” [1]. If the word “Pethuel” in Hebrew means “God opens,” then he begot “Joel,” which means: “Yahweh is God.” It is as though, when God opens our inner sight, He declares Himself to us. He is Yahweh! That is, “He who is”! God is the One beside whom all become as though they were not. For at God's first meeting with the first leader of the people, He said to him: “Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, The LORD God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, hath sent me unto you: this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial unto all generations” (Ex 3:15).
As Philo the Jew of Alexandria says, commenting on God's words to Moses: [Tell them first that I am He who is, so that you may know the difference between what is and what does not exist].

Let there be a Pethuel within us, that is, let God open our inner sight so that we may grasp His mysteries. Then we turn toward Him and are present with Him as the eternal Being. And let us not turn our back to Him lest we return to nothingness, for St. Augustine says: [Whoever takes the direction opposed to God is walking toward nothingness].
After this very brief introduction he speaks to them of the locust raids, saying:
Hear this, ye old men.
And give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land.
Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers?!
Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation (age).
That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten;
and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten;
and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpillar eaten. [2-4]

If the prophet asks the elders to listen to the word of the Lord, he asks all the inhabitants of the land to give ear, for God wishes to speak with all men without partiality!! Whether God speaks in one language or another, He seeks to meet with every person in order to declare His dealings of love with him.

The prophet also asks them to tell their children of the matter, that is, of the voice of the Lord and His dealings, so that they may hand on a life experience to the coming generation, and so each generation hands on to another what it has received. This is the “handing down” or “tradition,” which is in essence “God's dealings with the children of men.” For this reason the Apostle Paul says: “Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do” (Phil 4:9). And St. Gregory bishop of Nyssa says: [For the proof of our worship that tradition (handing down) suffices, which has come down to us from the Fathers, as the inheritance passed on by succession from the Apostles through the saints who followed them]... So every generation is bound to hand on to the new generation the Gospel of the Lord as the mystery of a practical life, through sound doctrine, living worship and spiritual conduct.

As for the locust raids mentioned here, most scholars have seen them as real invasions that the prophet witnessed, while some have thought them merely a visionary expression revealing what would be fulfilled later, especially in the last times...
The palmerworm is the locust when it comes out of its egg, unable to move.
The locust (the crawler) is the locust when it begins to move, so that it crawls or walks.
The cankerworm is the locust when two small wings sprout on it.
The caterpillar is the locust that sets off to fly in the air.

Many Jewish scholars, down to the days of St. Jerome, held that these four raids point to four campaigns made by Sennacherib king of Assyria against Judah (Isa 36:1), or to four kingdoms that ruled Israel and Judah, namely: Assyria and Babylon; the Medes and Persians; the Macedonians; the Romans; or: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon and Greece... At all events, the early Church accepted the symbolic understanding of these campaigns without denying that they took place.
In these four campaigns (the palmerworm, the locust, the cankerworm, the caterpillar) the following is to be observed:

First: we know that the number 4 points to the world with its four quarters: east, west, north and south, and to the body taken from the earth, that is, from the world. It is as though these raids represent the war of the love of the world against the believer, and the assault of the lusts of the flesh against the spirit. When man falls under sin, God permits him to be chastened through his very sin, since sin carries within itself its own corruption and bitterness. So the believer who turns aside toward the love of the world and the lusts of the flesh, God permits Himself to leave him for a time to the assaults of the love of the world and the lusts of the flesh, that the believer may realize that sin carries its corruption within it, and so be chastened by the very error he committed. This is what God constantly affirms to us: that the chastening that comes upon us is the natural fruit of a deed we committed, as He says: “Hast thou not procured this unto thyself?” (Jer 2:17). “Thy way and thy doings have procured these things unto thee; this is thy wickedness, because it is bitter, because it reacheth unto thine heart” (Jer 4:18). For when a man forsakes the true God and attaches himself to the love of the vain world and the temporary lusts of the flesh, he can expect nothing but to become vain himself, losing all that is true.
Judah loved the world and not God, the lusts of the flesh and not the spirit; therefore it became earth and not heaven, a body without a spirit.

Out of God's love for us, since we accept by our own will to become earth and not heaven, He permits violent temporal earthly calamities, volcanoes, earthquakes, floods, torrents, storms, plagues, famine, locust raids, and material losses that shake our earth, so that we leave it, fleeing to God, who alone renews our earth and makes it His heaven!!

If our earth, that is, our body, has borne of itself fleshly lusts, God permits and sends the locust raids as the natural fruit of our sins, to shatter what we thought to be joyful fruit. So we flee to God, who alone is able to sanctify us. He strips us of our own evil works, not to destroy us, but to destroy the evil that has dwelt in us and taken the center of our heart. He drives out evil that He Himself may reign in us, granting us by His Holy Spirit new fruit worthy of the new man. Therefore it is no wonder that the book begins with locust invasions to announce the Holy Spirit's invasion of our hearts (Joel 2:28-32), as we lose the fruit of the old man and his dead works and enjoy the fruit of the new man at a surpassing divine level!!
Lord, allow Your chastenings to me, however bitter, for as I feel through them the bitterness of my sins, my soul clings to the work of Your Holy Spirit, the Giver of life, who dwells in me!!

God showed Solomon the Wise the purpose of the chastening by locust raids, saying: “If I shut up heaven that there be no rain, or if I command the locusts to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among my people; if my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chr 7:13-14). He permits the locust not to destroy us, but to destroy our evil, so that we seek His face and respond to His Holy Spirit who dwells in us, and so receive forgiveness of sins. But alas, man often stubbornly resists himself, as the children of Israel did, when He rebukes them, saying: “When your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me” (Amos 4:9).

Second: God begins His chastening of man by permitting the raid of the little palmerworm to attack us. If we do not return to Him, He permits the locust; if we do not repent, the cankerworm and then the caterpillar; and when we do not accept all these chastenings, He permits the invasion of enemies. And finally the day of the Lord comes as a dense darkness for the one who has not accepted all kinds of chastening. He proceeds gradually with us in His chastenings so that when we submit to Him He may have mercy on us.

Third: perhaps this succession of locust stages, the palmerworm, the locust, the cankerworm and the caterpillar, points to the war of sin against us and its invasion of the heart. It begins with the very small palmerworm, which creeps secretly into the heart, the mind or the senses, like the little foxes that spoil the vines (Song 2:15), which man makes light of, so that they reign over the heart and corrupt it. And when the palmerworm plays its hidden part, the door is opened to the locust, where other sins crawl to us, so that one sin hands us over to another, and we become a plaything in their hands. And when the locust draws us into new sins we never thought we would fall into, the enemy grows bold against us, and more hideous and bitter sins seep in, representing sins in their ugliest form, that is, the caterpillar, which launches us into the depths of the abyss. This is what the Book of Revelation (Rev 9:1-12) describes as coming out of the pit of the abyss, darkening the light of the sun, stinging like a scorpion, with a sound like the sound of chariots of many horses running to battle. In other words, every slackness draws us on to a more dangerous stage until man yields to the destroying locust of the abyss. St. Mark the Ascetic says: [Satan offers us small sins that seem trivial in our eyes, because without this he cannot lead us to the great sins].

5 Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth. 6 For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion. 7 He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare, and cast it away; the branches thereof are made white. 8 Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth. 9 The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests, the LORD's ministers, mourn. 10 The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted: the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth. 11 Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen; howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is perished. 12 The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men.
Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth. [5]

At the beginning he asked them to hear and give ear. But now that the locust raids have come, he asked them to awake and come out of their drunkenness, since they had drunk the wine of the world that corrupted their mind and shattered their true wisdom. It is fitting for them to sober up from drunkenness in order to weep and howl over the deprivation they have come to!!

[There is a drunkenness of the soul that is hard to avoid, since the concerns of this world catch us even if we live a life of solitude. Of such the prophet says: “Awake, ye drunkards (but not with wine).” And another says: “They are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink” (Isa 29:9). In this drunkenness they use a wine which the prophet calls: “the poison of asps”...
Do you want to know something about the fruit of the vines and the fruit of that branch?

He says: “Their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter.” For unless we are purified from all errors, and renounce the surfeit of all lusts, we weigh down our hearts with a more dangerous intoxicant and wine. Without being drunk with wine or surfeited with feasts].
They became drunk with the wine of the love of the world, and so deprived themselves of the new wine, which is “the Holy Spirit,” by whom the soul reels in the love of God.

He calls them drunkards, and at the same time requires them to weep and howl over the new wine because it is cut off from their mouths. For they deprived themselves of what the disciples enjoyed on the day of Pentecost (the wine of the Holy Spirit), when the Apostle Peter stood and said: “For these are not drunken, as ye suppose, seeing it is but the third hour of the day. But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh...” (Acts 2:15-17).

Let old Israel weep and howl, because the new heavenly wine has been cut off from its mouth by their refusal of the Spirit's dwelling in them; and let the new Israel, the men of the New Testament, rejoice and exult, since they have rejected the wine of the world, that is, the works of the old man, in order to enjoy the wine of the life-giving Spirit!

When He asks those drunk with the wine of the world to awake and come to their senses because the locust raids have fallen upon them, He reveals to them the effect of these raids in many respects, in that they expose the work of sin in us.

He says, “For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion” [6]. The locust at any stage of its growth is no more than a small insect that a man can crush with his foot or even with his finger; yet locusts gather together as strong and dangerous campaigns that cannot be resisted.

In rebuke He says, “come up upon my land.” What befalls us because of our sins, although by divine permission for our chastening, He counts as touching His own land, for we are God's earth that He established for righteousness to dwell in (2 Pet 3:13). What we commit of sins wrongs God in His own land!

The secret of the strength of this nation without number lies in its mouth, for He says: “whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion.” The strange serpent opened its mouth to speak with Eve, and when she grew slack she perished, and her husband and her offspring also. Let us therefore beware of the words of the deceiving devil, let us flee from them as from the teeth of a lion and the cheek teeth of a lioness, for the wise man says of the wisdom of God: “That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words” (Prov 7:5).

It is fitting that we not be deceived by the devil's honeyed words lest they tear us apart, and also fitting that we keep watch lest the enemy of good use us, so that we ourselves become his teeth, which are like the teeth of a lion; he uses us in tearing apart the lives and faith of others. If the enemy of good, the devil, walketh about, as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet 5:8), let us not be his instrument in tearing apart our brethren.

Whoever hands his mouth over to the devil is like the teeth in the mouth of the destroying lion, as St. John Climacus says: [Peter opened his mouth with a word and wept bitterly, because he did not remember the saying: “I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue” (Ps 38:1), nor the other saying: “Better to slip from a roof than to slip with the tongue,” Ben Sira (Sir 20:20)].

And whoever hands his mouth over to the Lord becomes like the teeth in the mouth of the Lion of the tribe of Judah, bearing the spirit of conquest, victory and life through bearing witness to Him; he does not tear apart the life of his brethren but tears apart the work of the devil that opposes the truth.

So all of us are teeth, either in the mouth of the lion who opposes the truth or in the mouth of the Lion who is the truth. As the wise man says: “A man's belly shall be satisfied with the fruit of his mouth; and with the increase of his lips shall he be filled. Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov 18:20-21).
Second: “He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree” [7].

If our slackness toward sin has corrupted our life, the land of the Lord, so that it has become a field for the invasion of the enemy of good, the nation without number, that devours as with the teeth of a lion and the cheek teeth of a lioness, then this has shattered the vine of the Lord and His fig tree.

The Lord calls His people His vine and His fig tree. The vine yields the grapes that pass with the Lord through the winepress, to bear the mark of His sufferings and enter with Him into the power of His resurrection; and the fig, with its sweet covering that holds great quantities of fine seeds, is a sign of the work of love and unity of the sweet Holy Spirit, who holds the members together without isolation or individualism...

Sin makes the vine and the fig tree lose their mark, that is, it destroys the work of the crucified Christ and of the Holy Spirit in us. Sin shatters the vine of the Lord and breaks His fig tree, so that believers do not accept the winepress with joy in order to offer new wine in the Kingdom of the Father, nor to walk in the spirit of love and unity, which is the work of the Holy Spirit.

God rejoices in His people, like a vine in the wilderness, or like a firstripe fig that satisfies His heart (Hos 9:10); but sin corrupts this vine and breaks this fig tree, and as it is stated in the Book of Habakkuk: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines” (Hab 3:17).
Third: “He hath made it clean bare, and cast it away; the branches thereof are made white” [7].

The work of the locust extended to the bark of the stem and the branches. They lost their bark and their branches became white. How strange, for whiteness points to purity and holiness: at the Transfiguration the Lord Christ appeared with His raiment white as the light (Mt 17:2), for they bore within them the Sun of Righteousness shining in His splendor in them. And at the holy tomb St. Mary Magdalene saw “two angels in white” (Jn 20:12). But the enemy, in trying to deceive, uses the white color in the case of leprosy as a sign of uncleanness (Lev 13:12-13).

So long as we have Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, as a refuge in whom we hide, and He dwells in us, we bear His whiteness like the light; but if we are removed from Him by our rejection of Him, we become branches without bark to protect them... with the whiteness of unclean leprosy. The whiteness of Christ lifts us up to heaven, where the heavenly mystery of our whiteness stands; but the whiteness of leprosy drives its owner outside the camp to live in isolation, tearing his clothes, with his head bare, covering his upper lip and crying: Unclean! Unclean! (Lev 13:36, 45).
Fourth: entering into a state of early widowhood, for He says: “Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth” [8].

When man commits sin he thinks he is satisfying his deprived soul and quenching the thirst of his body with pleasures, but in truth he leads it into a state of widowhood, and it girds itself with sackcloth against its will, because it has lost its first bridegroom, “God,” to whom it was joined from its youth; and in place of the wedding garment that rejoiced it and the heavenly ones, it has the mournful sackcloth of widowhood.

In any case her first bridegroom, the husband of her youth, remains, coaxing her and bringing her into the wilderness and speaking comfortably to her (Hos 2:14), to take off her dark garment of widowhood, saying to her: “And I will betroth thee unto me for ever” (Hos 2:19). But He does not betroth her while she is in the bosom of the other man; rather He assures her: “I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD” (Hos 2:19-20).

Fifth: the cutting off of the offering and the drink offering, for He says: “The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests, the LORD's ministers, mourn” [9].

The raids of divine chastening reveal what the soul has come to because of sin: having become a widow, it lost its union with the heavenly Bridegroom, and the priests are no longer able to offer an offering or pour out a drink offering to the Lord, for He does not accept the offering of the wicked, nor the drink offering of those who have given Him the back and not the face.

The acceptance of the offering and the drink offering in the house of the Lord is a sign of union between God and His holy people and of God's good pleasure in them; but now that the people have fallen into abominations, there is no acceptance of their offerings without repentance and return to Him. The psalmist says: “For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:16-17).

In our study of the Second Epistle of our teacher the Apostle Paul to Timothy we saw that the drink offering points to the life of continual joy that the Holy Spirit pours out abundantly amid the sufferings of the Church, as the sacrifice of God united with Christ the Sacrifice. It is as though the cutting off of the drink offering is the removal of constant spiritual joy from the people so that gloom takes its place... This is the natural fruit of sin.

We need God to accept the offering and the drink offering... so that we bear the mark of the crucified Christ: the offering, and the mark of spiritual joy (the drink offering), if we return to Him by repentance.

Sixth: the ruin of the fruits: “The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted: the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth. Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen; howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is perished. The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men” [10-12].
If sin has corrupted the vine of the Lord and broken His fig tree, it destroys all spiritual fruit in the life of the believer, who is the field of the Lord.

A. The field is wasted, the new wine (the new bread) dried up, and the oil languishes: if the corn points to the necessary daily bread, then the new wine points to the joyful spiritual drink while the oil points to medicine. Thus the locust of sin deprives man of his spiritual food, drink and medicine, so that he lives in a state of hunger, thirst and sickness, with none to satisfy him, give him drink or bind up his wounds.

God withholds nothing from man, but man in his ignorance uses what is God's for the account of His enemy. God reproaches His bride, saying to her: “For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal” (Hos 2:8). “My meat also which I gave thee, fine flour, and oil, and honey, wherewith I fed thee, thou hast even set it before them (before male images with whom she commits adultery) for a sweet savour” (Ezek 17:19).

Would that through God's chastenings we realize what our inner state has come to, so that we hunger and thirst after righteousness (Mt 5:6). Then we find the Lord Christ a heavenly bread for us (Jn 6:15), and a spiritual drink, and a balm for our souls.

B. The husbandmen are ashamed and the vinedressers howl when the Lord of the harvest comes and finds His field without wheat or barley. He finds His shepherds and priests not offering the food of the rich (the wheat) or even the food of the poor (the barley).

If wheat is used as food for man and barley as food for animals, then sin corrupts everything, so that neither man (the human soul) is satisfied nor even the animal (the body); and man lives in a state of emptiness and hunger, spiritual, psychological and bodily as well.
C. There is found in the soul, the divine field, no fruit, whether pomegranate, palm or apple.

The pomegranate points to the meekness of Christ, which is reflected on the face of the Church His bride, so that the Lord says to her: “Thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks” (Song 4:3), since her face has His true meekness.
The palm points to the life of uprightness without deviation, as the Bridegroom says to His bride who bears the upright nature of her Bridegroom: “This thy stature is like to a palm tree” (Song 7:7).

And the apple points to the Incarnation, which bears fruit that gladdens the Father and men, where the bride says to her Bridegroom who became man: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste” (Song 2:3). So by the Holy Spirit, when we are united with the unique apple tree among the trees of the unfruitful wood, we ourselves become apples that gladden the heart of God and men, having the fragrance of our Christ... “the smell of thy nose like apples” (Song 7:8).
In other words, the absence of pomegranates, palms and apples means the removal from the human soul of the mark of Christ, His uprightness and His fragrance!

D. If sin deprives man of his spiritual food (the wheat), his drink (the new wine) and his medicine (the oil), makes him without fruit for soul and body (wheat or barley), and deprives him of the features of the Lord, His uprightness and His sweet fragrance... then all this deprives man of his spiritual gladness and inward joy, for He says: “because joy is withered away from the sons of men” [12].

Many think that a pampered life is joy and gladness, and that life with God is sorrow and gloom... But the truth is otherwise, for the pampered life carries inward bitterness and gloom amid its luxury and laughter, while life with God offers deep spiritual joy amid sufferings and afflictions. Sin deprives man of his spiritual joy, while repentance grants joy amid tears, and inward peace despite the narrow way and the strait gate. For this reason St. John Climacus wrote a whole discourse on “joy-bearing mourning,” in which he says: [Hold fast with all your might to the joyful sorrow that accompanies compunction of the heart, and do not cease from it, until it lifts you above earthly things and presents you pure to Christ], [He who has put on the blessed mourning, given to him as a wedding garment, has known the laughter of the spiritual soul], [Tears that come from the remembrance of death give birth to fear; when fear has given birth to confidence, joy shines forth; and when joy has grown calm and remained steady, the flower of holy love blossoms].

13 Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is withholden from the house of your God. 14 Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the LORD your God, and cry unto the LORD,
God revealed through His chastenings the bitter fruit of sin in the life of His people:
* A strong nation, without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, attacked His land [6].
* His vine became waste, and His fig tree barked [7].
* The stem and branches lost their bark and became without protection [7].
* His bride entered into a state of early widowhood [8].
* The offering and the drink offering were cut off, which are a sign of God's good pleasure and joy in His house [9].
* She lost food, drink and medicine [10].
* She lost the marks of the Lord, His uprightness and His sweet fragrance [12].
* She lost spiritual gladness [12].

And now the Lord hastens to turn tears and grief into repentance, which the priests must practice with the people, for He says: “Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is withholden from the house of your God...” [13]. He addresses the priests, the ministers of the altar, to take up their leading role, not by counsel and guidance, but first by practicing repentance in deed, so as to be with the people, not isolated from them. He has set forth the signs and features of repentance in the following points:

First: girding [13], or wearing sackcloth. It is not a time to wear costly and splendid priestly garments, but a time to gird oneself with sackcloth so that God may soften toward His people and have compassion on His fallen children. Wearing sackcloth is accompanied by inward humbling and contrition of spirit before God. St. John Climacus says: [Let your garment at least be a call to mourning, for all who mourn their dead wear black].

Second: mourning and howling [13]. It is fitting that the priest not ask for the tears of his brethren and spiritual children while dry in his own feelings, but practice what he asks of them, saying with the prophet: “For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I am black; astonishment hath taken hold on me... Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!” (Jer 8:21; 9:1).

St. John Climacus tells us of the power of mourning and tears, saying: [As fire consumes reeds, so a pure tear consumes every defilement of body and spirit], [God, my beloved, does not need a man to weep and groan, and does not want that, but rather wishes him to rejoice and exult in His love. Remove sin, O man, and the painful tear in the bodily eyes becomes a superfluous surplus, for there is no need of cleansing where there is no wound. Adam had no tears before the transgression, and there will be no tears after the resurrection, when sin will have been destroyed and with it pain, grief and sighing have passed away].

Third: sanctifying a fast for this purpose, for repentance touches the whole life of man, especially the priest: the sighs of his heart, the cry of his mouth, his clothes, and also his belly. It is as though man speaks with God, declaring his repentance by every means, so that his actions together support the declaration of his longing to return to God.
Fasting is the language of the bowels interacting with the spirit, mind and senses to declare the desire to meet God through the holy life in Him.

St. John Climacus says: [The mind of the one who fasts prays with pure thoughts, but the mind of the glutton is filled with unclean images], [Stuffing the stomach dries up the springs of tears, but if the stomach is dried by abstinence, those waters well up], [If we constrain our stomach, our heart is humbled; and if we indulge it, our mind becomes arrogant].
And Father Mar Isaac the Syrian says: [One of the saints said: When the body is weakened by fasting and mortification, the soul is strengthened spiritually by prayer].

Fourth: calling a solemn assembly. For He says to the priests: “call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the LORD your God, and cry unto the LORD” [14]. Thus the prophet declares the obligation to call a solemn assembly, that is, a communal celebration of repentance; for as the community shared together in the evil, so it shares in repentance. We spoke in the introduction to the Book of Hosea of communal repentance, which works together with personal spiritual life and the hidden relation between the soul and God, in that the soul is a member of the holy community.

If the priest represents the leading faculty in man, it is fitting that this leadership call a solemn assembly and gather the elders of all the inhabitants of the land; that is, that man gather all his senses, energies and abilities as though they were the elders of the land, that is, those working in the body, so that man may offer a repentance springing from all his actions and his spiritual, psychological and bodily capacities. Let the priests gather with the inhabitants of the land in the house of the Lord, that is, let the spirit with its energies work with the body with its energies under the leadership of the Lord, and let man cry with his whole being to his God.

Let the solemn assembly be held in the house of the Lord our God, so that we flee from God's wrath by taking refuge in Him and finding shelter in His tender love and longsuffering. As it is written in the Book of Isaiah: “Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me” (Isa 27:5).

15 Alas for the day! for the day of the LORD is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come. 16 Is not the meat cut off before our eyes, yea, joy and gladness from the house of our God? 17 The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered. 18 How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate. 19 O LORD, to thee will I cry: for the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame hath burned all the trees of the field. 20 The beasts of the field cry also unto thee: for the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness.

When the priests gather with the elders in the house of the Lord, all mourn and howl, realizing what sin has done in them, awaiting the One who alone is able to intercede for them with His atoning blood, and rescue them from the divine wrath on that dreadful day. The prophet has brought out these two complementary matters: realizing the bitterness and terror we have come to in view of the day of the Lord, and the need for an intercessor able to reconcile us with God.

As for realizing what we have come to, he says: “Alas for the day! for the day of the LORD is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come. Is not the meat cut off before our eyes, yea, joy and gladness from the house of our God? The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered. How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate” [15-18].

In short, we have come into a state of hunger, for the food has been cut off before our eyes; for the soul will not be satisfied with anything other than God Himself, in whose image and likeness it was created. Perhaps for this reason the Lord Christ, the incarnate Word of God, was born in a manger, so that when man became like a hungry beast he would incline to the manger, and acquire a new food able to satisfy him eternally. He hears Him say: “I am that bread of life... I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world... Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (Jn 6:48-53).

The food is cut off and joy and gladness are gone, so the soul is in gloom, indeed in a death in which it cannot say: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Hab 3:18)... because it has itself cut itself off from God, the source of its gladness.

The soul has come into a state of ruin without spiritual fruit, so the seed is rotten under its clods, and the barns are broken down, and it is without hope... even the beasts (the body) groan, the flocks of sheep are made desolate. By sin man loses even the bodily things for whose sake he committed it!

In other words we say that by sin the curse came upon everything, even upon the earth, as the Lord said to Adam: “cursed is the ground for thy sake” (Gen 3:17)... so there was no longer any place for blessing.

Now, after realizing the curse that has come upon us and upon the earth with its plants and animals, Joel enters as an intercessor, or more precisely as a symbol of the true Intercessor, Jesus Christ, who alone cries to His Father and is answered. He says, “O LORD, to thee will I cry.” He does not cry for himself but for the people, for the pastures that the fire has devoured, and for the rivers of waters that are dried up [19-20].

This is the Intercessor who dwells in the heart, the “inner Jerusalem,” and makes peace for the soul and body with all their energies with the Father. He in whom the Father rejoices and whom He seeks, saying: “Run ye to and fro through the streets of Jerusalem, and see now, and know, and seek in the broad places thereof, if ye can find a man, if there be any that executeth judgment, that seeketh the truth; and I will pardon it” (Jer 5:1). He is our Lord Jesus Christ, hidden in our inner Jerusalem, through whom we receive pardon for our sins!
Instead of locust raids, grant me Your fiery Spirit!
* Count me, Lord, like Joel, a son of Pethuel (God opens)!
Open, Lord, my heart, that I may see You within me, know You, and grasp Your wisdom!
* The sins of Judah brought upon their land the four locust raids:
the raids of the palmerworm, the locust, the cankerworm and then the caterpillar.
My sins have brought upon me Your chastenings, growing harsher by degrees, that perhaps I may turn back and repent!
My sins have turned my heart into a land of drought.
Instead of locust raids, let Your Holy Spirit descend on the land of my heart, and turn my wilderness into a fruitful paradise.
Turn my earth into a heaven which not one locust approaches!
* Chasten, Lord... and strengthen Your hand!
But do not allow my destruction, but the destruction of the corruption that has crept into me!
You allow me bitterness, but You seek the gladness of my salvation and my eternal joy!
* Sin has caused me drought and hunger!
It has corrupted my peace and removed my inner joy!
It has turned my wedding into a funeral!
It has removed Your sweet fragrance from my depths!
It has deprived me of the offering and the drink offering of joy!
It has removed the blessing from me and brought its curse upon me!
Who can save me from it but You, Savior of the world, my heavenly Intercessor!
You are my satisfaction, my peace, my joy, and the source of every blessing!

1 Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand; 2 A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains: a great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations. 3 A fire devoureth before them; and behind them a flame burneth: the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness; yea, and nothing shall escape them. 4 The appearance of them is as the appearance of horses; and as horsemen, so shall they run. 5 Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains shall they leap, like the noise of a flame of fire that devoureth the stubble, as a strong people set in battle array. 6 Before their face the people shall be much pained: all faces shall gather blackness. 7 They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks: 8 Neither shall one thrust another; they shall walk every one in his path: and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded. 9 They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief. 10 The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining: 11 And the LORD shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?

The people did not benefit from the locust raids, for it was said by the prophet Amos: “I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amos 4:9). So he began to speak to them of another chastening, the destructive raids of enemies, saying:
Blow ye the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain: let all the inhabitants of the land tremble: for the day of the LORD cometh, for it is nigh at hand. [1]

First: blowing the trumpet in Zion. Sounding trumpets was part of the very work of the priests; they were sounded when the procession moved “in the wilderness,” at the announcement of war, at the anointing of the king, at the celebration of feasts, etc... The trumpet was of silver (Lev 10) and points to the divine commandment or the divine word, which works in the soul during its striving and its war against sin and fills it with joy and gladness with every inner divine work.

God commands the blowing of the trumpet in Zion not because a particular nation is attacking Zion, but because the day of the LORD is coming, so that all the inhabitants of the land tremble... It is a near day!!

Perhaps by the blowing of trumpets in Zion, on the holy mountain, He wanted to declare that it is God who permits the enemies to rage against His people to chasten them. If they do not listen to His voice through the commandment, He brings them terror through their enemies, using them to accomplish their deliverance from evil; they did not listen to His meekness, so let them await His firmness!

Let us hear the sound of the trumpet, God's warnings, from the mouth of the priests, and let us accept the divine commandment even if it is bitter to the wicked, because it shatters the evil they love, for “all the inhabitants of the land tremble”; everything earthly is shaken in the heart of the wicked before the divine commandment, and every transgression and trespass within him quakes before it. As it was said: “Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid?!” (Amos 3:6).

If the blowing of the trumpet points to the coming of the divine Word to the soul, this is necessarily followed by the shattering of every inner idol that has occupied the heart for a time, as Isaiah the prophet says: “Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it” (Isa 19:1).
Second: “A day of darkness and of gloominess, a day of clouds and of thick darkness, as the morning spread upon the mountains” [2].

If the day of the Lord for true believers is a joyful and radiant wedding day, when the Bridegroom, the Sun of Righteousness, comes forward to meet His bride who shines like the moon with His light, then for the wicked it is a day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness, for they cannot behold the Lord in His glory and splendor, nor enjoy His mysteries.

The prophet Joel looks at the periods of the locust invasion and sees the sky turned into pitch darkness, not because the sun is absent, but because of the locusts that covered the whole sky, so that man lost the sight of the light, and day turned to night in his eyes. This scene was described in the Book of Exodus at the plague of locusts on the land of Egypt: “And the locusts went up over all the land of Egypt... For they covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened” (Ex 10:14-15).

Through this scene the prophet Joel saw what would happen in Judah by the armies of the enemies. Because of the multitude of the fighting army and the chariots, the land of Judah turns into a dust storm causing gloom and darkness. In the same image the matter is fulfilled for the wicked on the great day of the Lord, when He comes to judge the world, so that for them it is gloom and darkness because of the gloom of sin and its darkness which they carried within them, which veils from them the sight of His splendor.
Perhaps the darkness and gloom point to the bitterness and distress that come upon the soul during chastening, so that man's eyes and his outlook on life are darkened!

As for His saying “as the morning spread upon the mountains,” it means the assurance of its happening. It is coming without fail for all men: the holy mountains and the unclean mountains. The holy mountains of Zion rejoice in it, and the mountains bearing the altars of Baal tremble before it!

Third: He presents to us a bitter and harsh picture of the opposing army in respect of the number of the fighters, their strength and their effectiveness, for He describes it thus: 1. “A great people and a strong; there hath not been ever the like, neither shall be any more after it, even to the years of many generations” [2]. 2. God in His longsuffering waits and is patient... but out of His love He is compelled to chasten. And when we do not respond, God seems harsh in His chastenings, so that when we fall under chastening we feel that it is unique in its pains and bitterness! It is the tender fatherhood for the salvation of the rebellious soul that is dying in its sins!

B. It does not stop at the multitude of numbers, but “the appearance of them is as the appearance of horses; and as horsemen, so shall they run. Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains shall they leap” [4-5]. He terrifies our eyes with its appearance, our ears with its voice. The eyes that found sin pleasant, slack in their spiritual striving, are terrified by the divine chastening, which they see as a violent horse that none can resist, and as horsemen running, so there is no time for slackness or delay. Its voice is dreadful and violent in the extreme, like the noise of chariots that reaches the tops of mountains; none escapes from it!

C. As for the work of the chastening, it exposes the work of sin in us. For it turns our inner garden into a wilderness: “A fire devoureth before them; and behind them a flame burneth: the land is as the garden of Eden before them, and behind them a desolate wilderness; yea, and nothing shall escape them” [3]. This fiery invasion, although in its depths it is a divine chastening, is the natural fruit of the work of sin, the destroying fire; whoever practices it embraces a fire that destroys him. This fire can be overcome only by the fire of the Holy Spirit, who turns the desolate wilderness into a joyful paradise. For by the fire of the Holy Spirit the fire of sin is destroyed, and by the fruit of the Spirit the heart is restored to its first state to become the joyful garden of God, so that the believer says to his Savior: “Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits” (Song 4:6).

If this book is the book of the dreadful day of the Lord for sinners whose paradise has turned into a wilderness, it is at the same time the book of the outpouring of the Spirit on the sons of men, who restores our nature to us and makes us a paradise for God instead of the wilderness we have become. For this reason St. Gregory bishop of Nyssa says to the catechumens shortly before their baptism: [You are outside paradise, O catechumens. You share with Adam your first father in his exile, and now the door is opened and you return to where you went out from].

If the prophet sees in sin a fire consuming stubble [5], then the fiery Spirit turns these ashes into a holy temple of the Lord. St. Cyril the Great says: [The baptized receives the Holy Spirit in him and truly bears the title of temple of God].

D. As for the plan, it is extremely well ordered: “they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks: neither shall one thrust another; they shall walk every one in his path: and when they fall upon the sword, they shall not be wounded” [7-8]. For the prophet saw the locust raids covering the sky completely. They set out to the fields and ate everything green in them, and crept into the houses through the windows. None can resist! And with all this he realized that each locust had its task for which it was sent. So no locust crowds its sister, nor moves except as far as God allowed it for the chastening. What happened was not a mere natural disaster without purpose, but carried a precise purpose in its whole as in its details. And the very same thing is repeated with the invasion of the enemies against Judah: the devastation that occurs is not without purpose, but everything is determined with the utmost precision!

God, who permitted the enemy to attack His people, is not hindered by the wall standing before him; the plan is accomplished and each enters his position, and if he falls among the weapons he is not wounded until he fulfills the purpose.

E. None escapes this chastening, since all have sinned. If it attacks the open fields in the villages and turns them into a wilderness, it creeps like thieves through the windows into the houses in the cities. It leaps over the wall and no barrier stands before it... None can flee, for the fruit of sin follows him wherever he is, even if he is inside his chamber surrounded by impregnable walls!

F. It carries the bitterness of myrrh, and none can bear it: “The earth shall quake before them; the heavens shall tremble: the sun and the moon shall be dark, and the stars shall withdraw their shining: and the LORD shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?! [10-11].

These are the very signs the Lord Christ Himself gave concerning His last coming; they are terrifying signs for wicked sinners... God permits nature to be shaken and to tremble before them so that they may realize what sin does to nature, and sinners prepare by repentance to meet the Lord.

And it is wonderful that God regards the army opposing His people as “His army,” because it is He who permitted it to carry out the chastening, so that it became His rod for chastening, but only for a time.

The Fathers have spiritual, symbolic understandings of the quaking of the earth, the trembling of the heavens, the darkening of the sun and moon and the falling of the stars... a matter to which we return at greater length in our study of the Gospel of Matthew (Mt 24), God willing and if we live, being content here with a few excerpts:

* Now is the end of all the passing life. As the Apostle says, the fashion of this outward world passes away, to be followed by a new world, and instead of the visible stars Christ Himself shines as the sun of the new creation and its king. Great is the power of this new sun. And great is His splendor, like the sun that now shines, where the moon and the other stars grow dark before this great light.

Eusebius of Caesarea * Just as the moon and the stars quickly dwindle before the rising sun, so before the appearing of Christ the sun is darkened, and the moon does not give its light, and the stars fall from heaven, so that their former splendor is taken from them that they may put on the garment of the great light.

St. John Chrysostom The trembling earth is the body, which grows weak and wasted before the abominations that man commits for the delight and ease of his body, so that while he thinks he is giving his body rest, he makes it tremble without knowing. And the heavens point to the soul, which should have been the center of the Kingdom of God and the place of His dwelling... The soul loses its security and peace through sin, and so trembles. And the heavenly lights cease, a sign of the loss of spiritual sight and entrance into a state of spiritual confusion. Thus the divine chastening declares the fruit of our sins; it exposes them in us, so that we cannot bear His dreadful day. The men of Beth-shemesh, who had looked into the ark of the covenant, said earlier: “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God? and to whom shall he go up from us?” (1 Sam 6:20). As the psalmist says: “Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry? Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, when God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth” (Ps 76:7-9).

12 Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: 13 And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil. 14 Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the LORD your God? 15 Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly: 16 Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children, and those that suck the breasts: let the bridegroom go forth of his chamber, and the bride out of her closet. 17 Let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep between the porch and the altar, and let them say, Spare thy people, O LORD, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God?

Having revealed through His chastenings the working of sin in soul and body, God opened wide the doors of hope to His people so that none should fall into despair. For He calls, saying: “Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: and rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil. Who knoweth if he will return and repent, and leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the LORD your God?” [12-14].
In this call He declares the following:

A. Repentance in its essence is “a return to God”... not merely remorse for sin or ceasing from iniquity, but in its positive aspect a return to the divine embrace, so that we give God the face and not the back... For this reason God affirms His own traits in His relationship with us: that He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and of great mercy.

As St. Cyprian says: [He can pardon, having compassion on the sinner who works while asking mercy]. God has used every possible means to express His love for man and His compassion for him so that he may return to Him and find in Him the fatherly embrace that is never closed before those who return! St. Ambrose says: [Let no one fear destruction, whatever his condition and however great his fall, for the good Samaritan of the Gospel will pass by him, and find him going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, that is, fleeing from the sufferings of martyrdom to enjoy the pleasures of the world, wounded by thieves... lying half dead; this good Samaritan, who is a symbol of the Lord Christ, who is the guardian of souls, will not leave you, but will have compassion on you and heal you].

If it is God who permits the chastening, which we regard as evil, then when we return to Him “he repenteth him of the evil.” As Father Theodore says: [Scripture is accustomed to use certain expressions in other than their original meaning, so it uses the word “evils” for “sorrows and afflictions,” not because they are evil or evil in nature, but because those upon whom these things come for their good regard them as evil. So when the divine judgment speaks with men, it speaks with them according to their language and human feelings].

B. Returning with all the heart: many return to God in time of distress but not with all the heart, so that when the distress is lifted they return at once to their former wickedness, and perhaps to a worse state, as was Pharaoh, who called Moses and Aaron and asked them to pray for him and his people, that he would let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD (Ex 8:8), but “when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the LORD had said” (Ex 8:15)...

Let our return to God be with all the heart, supported in this by fasting, weeping and mourning... It is as though the body shares with the soul in returning to God, declaring this by prayer, fasting and tears.

On this St. Ambrose says: [Would that those who repent knew how to offer repentance, with what zeal and what feelings, and how it swallows up all his thinking, shakes his inner bowels, and pierces the depths of his heart, for Jeremiah the prophet says: “Behold, O LORD; for I am in distress: my bowels are troubled; mine heart is turned within me” (Lam 1:2)].

And he says: [“The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, and keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground. Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth” (Lam 2:10-11). So also the people of Nineveh grieved and so escaped the destruction of their city (Jonah 3:5). How great is the power of this medicine of repentance, so that it seems to change the intention of God!].

[Show your wounds to the Physician and He will heal you... Remove the traces of your wounds with tears! For this is what the woman mentioned in the Gospel did, and so removed the stench of her sins. She washed her sins by washing the feet of the Savior with her tears].

Repentance does not stop at the outward appearance, but must touch the inner heart, the whole heart... “Rend your heart, and not your garments.” As St. Cyprian says: [I ask you, dear brethren, that each one confess his sins which he committed in this world... Let us return to the Lord with all the heart, and express our repentance for our sins by true sorrow, beseeching the mercy of God, that our souls may bow before Him, that our sorrow may intercede before Him, that all our hope may be in Him, for He has told us how to ask Him... Let us return to the Lord with all our heart, and quench His anger and wrath by fasting, weeping and mourning, as He Himself advised us].

C. His saying: “Who knoweth if he will return and repent” does not mean uncertainty, but is a sign of standing before God with humbling and contrition, hoping for His mercy; for God asks humility in our repentance, since “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:17).

He repents, not in the sense of a change of God's mind, but in the sense of love, like a father who chastens his son firmly, pretending to be harsh in the hope that his son will return to him, and so he returns to his son. Even in the moments of his firmness he cannot bear the son's tears. And the sign of his repentance is that he leaves behind the chastening a blessing and not wrath, and accepts from his son the offering and the drink offering as a sign of his good pleasure in him and acceptance of him: “leave a blessing behind him; even a meat offering and a drink offering unto the LORD your God” [14].

D. Repentance is practiced by the whole community, the elders, the children, the infants, the newly married, the priests and the ministers of the LORD. If sin has extended to all, it is fitting that all take part together, and that the building support one another in the life of repentance.

The prophet Jeremiah speaks of what sin did to the infants: “The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them” (Lam 4:4)... And in God's mercy toward Nineveh the children had their own special regard with Him, for He says: “And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?!” (Jn 4:11).

E. The priests share with the people in repentance as ministers of the LORD between the porch and the altar, whose principal work is serving the Lord through the altar, that is, in Christ the Sacrifice. They serve through constant prayer and intercession for the people, saying: “Spare thy people, O LORD, and give not thine heritage to reproach, that the heathen should rule over them: wherefore should they say among the people, Where is their God?!” [17].

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: 18 Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people. 19 Yea, the LORD will answer and say unto his people, Behold, I will send you corn, and wine, and oil, and ye shall be satisfied therewith: and I will no more make you a reproach among the heathen: 20 But I will remove far off from you the northern army, and will drive him into a land barren and desolate, with his face toward the east sea, and his hinder part toward the utmost sea, and his stink shall come up, and his ill savour shall come up, because he hath done great things. 21 Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice: for the LORD will do great things. 22 Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring, for the tree beareth her fruit, the fig tree and the vine do yield their strength. 23 Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month. 24 And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the vats shall overflow with wine and oil. 25 And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpillar, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you. 26 And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed. 27 And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.

“Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people” [18]... What God permitted His people of suffering was out of His jealousy for His holy land, and His tenderness toward His people who are very dear to Him, for while He chastens, He asks His children to look to Him not as an avenging judge but as a loving Father who longs to rejoice in them and delight in their love for Him. The signs of His fatherly love are:

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: A. If the soul enters a state of hunger, thirst and sickness because of sin, God in His love offers Himself as food, drink and spiritual medicine to it, saying: “Behold, I will send you corn, and wine, and oil, and ye shall be satisfied therewith: and I will no more make you a reproach among the heathen” [19]... It no longer asks the Gentiles, that is, the world, to satisfy its emotion, quench its senses or heal its wounds, but finds in its Bridegroom all satisfaction.
St. John Saba addresses God, the source of true satisfaction, saying:
[Blessed is he who has forgotten the talk of the world by his talk with You, for from You all his needs are fulfilled!
You are his food and his drink!
You are his house and his dwelling of rest; into You he enters at all times to be sheltered!
You are his sun and his day; by Your light he sees hidden things!
You are the Father who begot him!

You have given the Spirit of Your Son in him, and the Spirit has given him boldness to ask from You all that is Yours, as a son asks of his father! His talk is with You at all times, for he knows no father but You!].

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: B. When God accomplishes the purpose by the chastening, in that the people return to Him, He judges the opposing people, the army that He used as an instrument of chastening... Why? Because it fell into pride, as the prophet says: “Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks” (Isa 10:12). The enemy acted arrogantly and thought himself mighty, and did not realize that God was using him to chasten His people. Therefore the Lord humbles him for his arrogance: “I will remove far off from you the northern army, and will drive him into a land barren and desolate, with his face toward the east sea (the Dead Sea, east of Judea), and his hinder part (his rear) toward the utmost sea (the western sea), and his stink shall come up, and his ill savour (his foul smell) shall come up, because he hath done great things” [20]...

Thus, when he falls into arrogance, the Lord splits him, to shatter his front in the waters of the Dead Sea and his rear at the farthest of the western sea so that they may not be gathered together again, and the smell of his stench rises in every place. All this is because of arrogance, as Isaiah the prophet says: “For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant man... Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire. And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day; and shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field (soul and body together)” (Isa 10:13-18).

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: C. The Lord washes their former wounds, turning the grief that overcame them because of sin into gladness and joy [21].

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: D. The sanctification of all energies and gifts by the Holy Spirit, for He says: “Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring, for the tree beareth her fruit, the fig tree and the vine do yield their strength. Be glad then, ye children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God: for he hath given you the former rain moderately, and he will cause to come down for you the rain, the former rain, and the latter rain in the first month” [22-23].

The Messianic age was linked in the minds of the prophets with holy waters (Ezek 36:26; Isa 30:23; Jer 31:9; Zech 13:1-2; Ps 46:4, etc.) that turn the wilderness into fertile land, water the believers like the trees of the paradise of God, remove uncleanness and purify the land from the worship of idols, and bring life and sanctification...

What is the former and latter rain but the Holy Spirit who waters the thirsty soul, so that the wilderness springs, the trees bear their fruit, and the fig tree and the vine yield their strength?! It is the Holy Spirit who worked in ancient times as the former rain, but much more settled in us after the Lord's ascension to turn our inner wilderness into a joyful paradise!

The prophet says: “Be not afraid, ye beasts of the field: for the pastures of the wilderness do spring.” If the body has become, because of sin, like the beasts of the field without pasture, the Holy Spirit sanctifies the body and satisfies all its energies and senses with what is for edification; He does not destroy the beasts of the field, nor despise their worth, but sanctifies them and satisfies them with what is of the Lord! For this reason He asks the children of Zion to be glad and rejoice because of this heavenly rain. It is as though the prophet declares through the shadow what the Lord said to His disciples: “Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you” (Jn 16:7).

This is the rain that the Lord Christ promised His disciples to send them from the Father as a sign of His love for them and care for them, and as it is written in Proverbs: “In the light of the king's countenance is life; and his favour is as a cloud of the latter rain” (Prov 16:15). And Hosea the prophet says: “His going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth” (Hos 6:3). And Zechariah the prophet asks us to ask for this latter rain to work in our lives: “Ask ye of the LORD rain in the time of the latter rain; so the LORD shall make bright clouds, and give them showers of rain, to every one grass in the field” (Zech 10:1). This is God's great gift: “Let us now fear the LORD our God, that giveth rain, both the former and the latter, in his season: he reserveth unto us the appointed weeks of the harvest” (Jer 5:24).

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: The Lord Christ gave us this latter rain in due time so that our souls may be satisfied with the Lord and praise Him, and realize His dwelling in their midst, that is, He gives them spiritual satisfaction and a life of praise and the sense of the divine presence, for He says: “And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed. And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed” [26-27].

Since man went out of paradise hungry, the whole world cannot satisfy his heart or his senses or his mind... so he remains wandering on the face of the earth in great hunger until God fills him with His satisfying Holy Spirit!

This satisfaction begets praise, so that man becomes like the infant who rejoices in his mother, so that all his feelings are stirred and all the members of his body respond with his joy to bring forth a song of true love that the tongue cannot express. For praise is not merely words we chant or melodies we learn, but in its depths it is a state of true joy that shakes the whole being of the believer, bodily and spiritually, so that the tongue breaks out in praise, and the heart dances with delight in the Lord, and the whole soul is stirred with heavenly, angelic melodies.

This praise is linked with the believer's awareness of the Lord's dwelling in him. He praises and exults not because of the gifts, even if they are spiritual, but because of the Giver Himself, the Giver of gifts!

These are the signs of God's fatherly love for His people. He satisfies the soul, waters it, binds up its wounds, restores to it its glory in Him, and removes from it the shame of sin and iniquity, sanctifying all its energies and gifts for His own account, declaring His dwelling in it as the mystery of its satisfaction and its spiritual praise!
The blessings of His love for His people can be summarized as follows:
A. He pities them, that is, has compassion and tenderness toward them [18].
B. He answers them and listens to them [19].
C. He satisfies their needs and grants them spiritual satisfaction [19].
D. He removes shame from them [19], granting them glory.
E. He drives out their enemies and shatters their pride [20].
F. He removes from them fear and anxiety [21].
G. He gives them gladness and joy [21].
H. He cares even for their beasts [22].
I. He blesses the fruit of their land [22].
J. He gives them the former and latter rain [23] (the gift of the Holy Spirit).
K. He compensates them for the years that the locust has eaten [24].
L. He gives them the spirit of praise and living spiritual worship [26].
M. He declares His wonders in their lives, so that they become a wonder [26].

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: N. He declares His dwelling in their midst [27].

entries.section: 3. God has pity on His people:

paragraphs.text: O. He gives them His Holy Spirit [28].

entries.section: 4. Radical reform by the Holy Spirit:

paragraphs.text: 28 And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions: 29 And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit. 30 And I will shew wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke. 31 The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come. 32 And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered: for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the LORD hath said, and in the remnant whom the LORD shall call.

entries.section: 4. Radical reform by the Holy Spirit:

paragraphs.text: When God pities His people and is jealous for His inheritance, He withholds nothing from them, but gives them Himself. He gives them His Holy Spirit in them as the mystery of their radical inner change, for He says: “And it shall come to pass (that is, in the last times) that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions: and also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit” [29].

It is the great gift that God gave to mankind after preparing for it by offering the sacrifice of redemption on the Cross. This gift which the Church enjoyed on the day of Pentecost, as the Apostle Peter declared (Acts 2:14-21), and which was offered to every man who comes to God, is God's gift to sons and daughters, that is, without distinction of sex on the one hand. And on the other hand it is given even to those of little experience, for it is the free gift from God to everyone who receives!
And it is God's gift to the old men whose lives have grown slack and who feel lost, for He turns their spiritual old age into youth renewed in the Lord, full of hope and joy.
It is God's gift to the servants and handmaids, given to those who realize that they are slaves, so that He frees them, granting them the spirit of sonship.
It is God's gift to the sons of men... that is, to all who receive!
As for the work of the Holy Spirit in us, it suffices to recall the words of St. Basil the Great: [Through the Holy Spirit is the restoration of our dwelling in paradise.
Our ascent to the Kingdom of Heaven.
Our return to divine sonship.
Our boldness to call God “our Father.”
Our sharing in the grace of Christ.
Our being called sons of light.
And in one word, our receiving the fullness of blessing in this age and in the age to come].

St. Ambrose comments on the phrase “I will pour out my spirit,” saying: [He did not say “I will pour out the Spirit” but “Of My Spirit,” for we cannot receive the fullness of the Holy Spirit, but we receive as much as our Lord apportions from Himself according to His will (Phil 2:6)]. But this does not mean that the Spirit does not dwell in us, nor that we receive a part of Him, for St. Clement of Alexandria warns us against dividing the Spirit; rather it is the mystery of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, working in us as God wills for our edification, in a surpassing divine manner.

entries.section: 4. Radical reform by the Holy Spirit:

paragraphs.text: This gift is accompanied by: “wonders in the heavens and in the earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come” [30]... It is as though the goal of this great gift is to launch the Church toward the great day of the Lord, to see heaven and earth pass away, the light of the world put out so that what is divine remains! By this her heart is set ablaze toward union with God alone, the Eternal!

entries.section: 4. Radical reform by the Holy Spirit:

paragraphs.text: Finally he closes his prophecy about the Holy Spirit by declaring His acceptance of all who come to Him from all the nations, for He says: “And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered” [32]. God opens His arms to everyone who calls on Him, whether Jew or Gentile, as the Apostle Paul says: “For the scripture saith, Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. For there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him. For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom 10:11-13). And as Peter says: “For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call” (Acts 2:39).

St. Augustine says: [The name of the Maker of heaven and earth was formerly called upon among the Israelites alone, while the rest of the nations called upon the dumb, deaf idols that do not hear, or called upon the demons, who hear what is to their harm]. But now the Gentiles have come to call on the name of the living God by the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: In the midst of Your chastenings I feel the tenderness of Your compassion!

paragraphs.text: * You permitted the four locust raids to chasten Your people, and when they did not benefit You sent them the raid of the Babylonians...
And in all this You are wonderful in Your love!
You pity Your people!
In the midst of Your chastenings I feel the tenderness of Your compassion!
* In the midst of Your chastenings I feel that Your day is a day of gloom, but You are behind the cloud!
Soon the cloud will lift and You will shine in me with Your splendor!
Allow me to see Your light amid my sufferings!
* Teach me how tender You are in Your love and compassion, so that I return to You not by rending my garments but by the contrition of my heart!
Against You only have I sinned; to You I disclose the wounds of my soul, O heavenly Physician!
Heal me, and I shall be healed!
Fill every void of my heart with Your love!
Send Your Holy Spirit to work in my depths!
Let Him turn my inner wilderness into a heavenly paradise!
How tender You are in Your love even in the moments of Your chastening of me!

entries.section: 1. The judgment of the wicked in the valley of Jehoshaphat:
